passages.text: At dawn Peter went out and stood at his usual place for discussion, where he saw a large crowd assembled. Just as he was about to speak, one of his attendants came in and said, ‘Simon has arrived from Antioch. Having learned last evening that you had promised to give a discourse on sole sovereignty, he is ready, together with Athenodorus the Epicurean, to come upon you while you speak and publicly oppose everything you say in any way in support of sole sovereignty.’ While the attendant was saying this, Simon himself came in with Athenodorus and some other companions. Before Peter could say anything, Simon spoke first:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ μοναρχίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: on sole sovereignty
lexical_decisions.rationale: The discussion concerns the rule of the one God, not a particular human monarchy. Sole sovereignty retains the political-rule image without replacing it everywhere by the broader modern term monotheism.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν αὐτοῦ διακόνων
lexical_decisions.chosen: of his attendants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes one who serves Peter. An ecclesiastical deacon is possible, but a formal office is not established by this occurrence alone.

passages.text: ‘I learned that yesterday you promised Faustus to demonstrate today, presenting your discourse in order and beginning with the Master of all himself, that he alone must be called God, that no others should be called or considered gods, and that whoever acts otherwise must be punished eternally. Above all, I am truly astounded at your recklessness in hoping to persuade a wise man, an old man at that, to your own wishes. But you will not achieve your designs, especially with me present here to expose your false arguments. Perhaps, had I not been present, the wise old man would have been deceived, since he is unfamiliar with the books publicly credited among the Jews. For now I will pass over lengthy arguments so as to expose your promise more quickly. Therefore begin to say what you promised in our own presence, for we know the scriptures. If, however, ashamed of exposure, you wish to pass over your promise in our presence, that too is sufficient proof that you are lying, because you did not dare to speak before those who know the scriptures. And why am I now waiting for you to speak, when I have the greatest witness to your promise in the old man standing here?’ Having said this, he looked directly at our father and said, ‘Tell me, most honored of all men, did not this man promise to demonstrate to you today that there is one God, that one should not call or consider anyone else a god, and that whoever acts otherwise, as one committing the greatest sin, must be punished eternally? Or will you not answer me?’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸν μόνον δεῖ λέγειν, ἄλλους δὲ μήτε λέγειν μήτε νομίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: he alone must be called God, that no others should be called or considered gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: God is the understood predicate supplied by the discourse and explicitly repeated later in the same passage. Both calling and regarding are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις δημοσίᾳ πεπιστωμένων βίβλων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the books publicly credited among the Jews
lexical_decisions.rationale: The books' accepted authority is attributed to the Jewish community in Simon's speech. Credited or held trustworthy is the sense, not a claim that their contents have already been proved in this debate.

passages.text: Our father said, ‘You would rightly demand testimony from me, Simon, if Peter had first denied it. As things stand, I will not be ashamed to say what needs saying. I think you want to debate while inflamed with anger, which is unfitting for you to do and for us to listen to. It means witnessing a quarrel, not being helped toward truth. Knowing from Greek education how inquirers should proceed, I will now remind you. Let each of you set out his own doctrine, and let your arguments be directed against the other. If Peter alone sets out his view while you keep yours silent, an argument you put forward might press against both his view and yours. Although both of you were defeated by the argument, you would not both appear defeated: the one who set out his view would, but the equal defeat of the one who did not set out his view would not be evident. He might even be thought to have won.’ Simon answered, ‘I will do as you say, but I fear that, having already been won over by his words, you will not be a truth-loving judge.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὀργῇ πεπρισμένον
lexical_decisions.chosen: inflamed with anger
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle can portray being cut or sawn through by anger. Inflamed is an idiomatic description of the resulting angry condition, not a claim about physical fire; cut through with anger is a more image-literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ εἰς ἕτερον οἱ λόγοι γενέσθωσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: and let your arguments be directed against the other
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reciprocal contrast of two speakers supports each directing argument toward the other. It does not require appointing an unnamed third interlocutor.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἀμφοτέρους ὑμᾶς ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἡττηθέντας μὴ φαίνεσθαι ἡττημένους
lexical_decisions.chosen: Although both of you were defeated by the argument, you would not both appear defeated
lexical_decisions.rationale: The next clauses specify that only the openly stated position would visibly lose. Both actual defeat and asymmetric appearance are retained, without changing the hidden position into a victorious one.

passages.text: Our father answered, ‘Do not force me to agree with you without judgment so that I may seem a truth-loving judge. If you wish to hear the truth, I am more predisposed toward your view.’ Simon said, ‘How are you predisposed when you do not know what I think?’ Our father said, ‘That is easy to know; listen to how. You promised to expose Peter as lying when he says there is one God. It is entirely clear that someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood does not, if he speaks truly, say the same thing. For if he says the same as the one accused of lying, he too lies. But if he demonstrates the opposite, then he speaks truly. You cannot, then, call the man who says there is one God a liar unless you believe there are many gods. I too say there are many gods. Since I agree with you before the inquiry, I am more predisposed toward you. In this respect you have no need to be anxious about me; Peter does, since I still think the opposite of him. After your inquiry, I hope, as a truth-loving judge who has stripped off preconception, to agree with the prevailing argument.’ When our father had said this, a subdued cry of praise arose from the crowds because he had argued in this way.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ καταψευδομένῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one accused of lying
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle can indicate one being lied against or falsely accused. In the debate's conditional argument, accused of lying follows the stated charge without independently certifying Peter as actually false.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρόληψιν ἀποδυσάμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: who has stripped off preconception
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clothing-removal image and the need to set aside a prior opinion are both retained, rather than changing the father's initial shared belief into an already completed conversion.

passages.text: Peter nevertheless said, ‘I am ready to do as the mediator of our discussion has said, and now, without any further delay, I will set out my view about God. I say that there is one God, who made heaven, earth, and everything in them. It is not permitted to call or consider anyone else a god.’ Simon said, ‘But I say that the scriptures trusted among the Jews speak of many gods, and that God is not angry at this, because he himself has spoken of many gods through his scriptures.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ τῶν λόγων μεσίτης
lexical_decisions.chosen: the mediator of our discussion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The role concerns moderation of the exchange, not a theological mediator between God and humanity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ αὐτὸν διὰ τῶν γραφῶν αὐτοῦ πολλοὺς θεοὺς εἰρηκέναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: because he himself has spoken of many gods through his scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The divine subject and possessive scriptures are retained as Simon's stated reason. They do not represent an independent translator's conclusion about scriptural authorship or polytheism.

passages.text: ‘Indeed, in the law's first utterance he even appears to speak of them as like himself. For it is written that the first human had received God's command to eat from every tree in the garden, but not to eat from the tree of knowing good and evil. The serpent, through the woman, persuaded them to eat on the promise that they would become gods, and caused them to see. Then, when they had come to see, God said to them, “Look, Adam has become like one of us.” Thus the serpent, saying, “You will be like gods,” appears to have spoken as though gods exist, all the more so since God too testified, saying, “Look, Adam has become like one of us.” So the serpent, who said that there are many gods, did not lie. Again, the writing, “You shall not speak evil of gods, and you shall not speak badly of the rulers of your people,” indicates many gods, of whom he does not even wish evil to be spoken. Elsewhere too it is written, “Has another god dared to go in and take for himself a nation from the midst of a nation, as I, the Lord God, have?” In saying, “Has another god dared,” he spoke as though others exist. And elsewhere, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish,” as those who did not make them are going to perish. Somewhere else it says, “Watch yourself, lest you go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,” as though other gods exist, whom he also tells them not to follow. And again, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” Here too he speaks of many gods, whose names he does not wish to be named. Again it is written, “The Lord your God, he is God of gods.” And again, “Who is like you, Lord, among gods?” And again, “God of gods, the Lord.” And again, “God stood in an assembly of gods, and in their midst he judges gods.” So I wonder how, when so many utterances testify in writing that there are many gods, you do not firmly assert that one must neither call them gods nor believe that they exist. For the rest, if you have anything to say in response to these clear statements, speak before everyone.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀναβλέψαι ἐποίησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: caused them to see
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean look up or regain sight. The ensuing Adam quotation and the related form ἀναβλέψασιν support their coming to sight or awareness here; opened their eyes is an idiomatic alternative but supplies an unexpressed anatomical object.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ἢ καὶ θεὸς ἐπεμαρτύρησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: all the more so since God too testified
lexical_decisions.rationale: The awkward comparative sequence is read as reinforcing the serpent's statement with God's corroboration. More literally, all the more in this respect—or even God testified. The main text makes the evidentiary link intelligible without changing who speaks or testifies.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ διαβεβαιοῦσαι μὴ δεῖν μήτε λέγειν μήτε εἶναι νομίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: you do not firmly assert that one must neither call them gods nor believe that they exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the printed οὐ and the subsequent prohibition's negatives are retained. The resulting question is rhetorically awkward in Simon's argument; the initial negative is not silently deleted or changed into a different Greek word to resolve the difficulty.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κύριος ὁ θεός
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Lord God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The quoted Greek title is translated Lord, not replaced by Yahweh, since this is the wording quoted by the ancient author rather than a fresh translation from a Hebrew divine-name occurrence.

source_issues.issue: This wording is supplied within editorial square brackets in the selected edition. The English translates that supplied wording, including the negative and the destruction clause; it is not an independent recovery or proof that the bracketed words survive unbroken in the underlying witness. There is no printed dotted gap here to invent or fill.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘Hear a briefer reply to what you have said. The law itself, which has often spoken of gods, itself says to the Jewish multitude, “Look, to the Lord your God belong the heaven of heaven and everything in them.” This includes the point that, even if gods exist, they are under him, that is, under the God of the Jews. Again, “For the Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other besides him.” Somewhere else scripture says to the Jewish multitude, “The Lord your God, he is God of gods,” as though to say that even if gods exist, they are under the God of the Jews. Elsewhere scripture says of him, “The great and true God, who shows no partiality and will accept no gift, rendering justice to orphan and widow.” In calling the God of the Jews great, true, and one who renders justice, scripture indicated that the others are small and not true. Elsewhere too scripture says, “As I live, says the Lord, there is no other god besides me. I am first; I am after these things; besides me there is no god.” Again, “You shall fear the Lord your God and worship him alone.” And again, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord.” Indeed, many utterances seal with an oath that God is one and that there is no god besides him. So I wonder how, when so many utterances testify that there is one God, you say there are many.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ οὐρανὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ πάντα ὅσα ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the heaven of heaven and everything in them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular heaven of heaven and the ensuing plural pronoun are preserved as quoted, rather than harmonized with a different scriptural form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ λαμβάνει πρόσωπον οὐδὲ μὴ λάβῃ δῶρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: shows no partiality and will accept no gift
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first idiom concerns favoritism rather than literally taking a face. The second names a gift in a judicial context, where bribe is a plausible explanatory alternative; the main wording keeps the source's expressed noun.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐγὼ πρῶτος, ἐγὼ μετὰ ταῦτα
lexical_decisions.chosen: I am first; I am after these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied expression after these things is translated rather than replaced with the familiar but unprinted title last.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Lord your God is one Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: The quoted word order permits the traditional one-Lord rendering or the Lord is one. The main rendering keeps the repeated Lord and the explicit numerical one, without importing a different creed or Hebrew wording.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘My argument with you from the beginning was to expose you from the scriptures as lying when you say one must not speak of many gods. That is why I showed many written utterances: the divine scriptures themselves speak of many gods.’ Peter said, ‘The very scriptures that speak of many gods also instructed us, saying, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” So I did not speak against what is written, Simon.’ Simon said, ‘Listen to a reply to that too, Peter. You seem to me to sin in speaking against them, since scripture says, “You shall not speak evil, and you shall not speak badly of a ruler of your people.”’ Peter said, ‘I do not sin, Simon, in foretelling their destruction in agreement with the scriptures. For it is written, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish.” This does not mean, as you interpreted it, that some did make them and will not perish. For the maker is shown to be one by what is written from the beginning: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” It did not say “the gods.” Somewhere else it says, “The firmament announces the work of his hands.” And in another place it is written, “The heavens themselves will perish, but you will remain forever.”’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παρήγεσαν ἡμῖν εἰποῦσαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: also instructed us, saying
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb presents the scriptures as providing the instruction that follows. They appeared before us is a more spatially literal alternative; the argument treats their quoted prohibition as the operative instruction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: στερέωμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: firmament
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes the established heavenly expanse in the quoted cosmological language. It is not modernized into a scientifically specified atmosphere or an otherwise unexpressed material dome.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘To show that there are many gods, I presented clear utterances from the scriptures. You have brought as many, or even more, utterances from those same scriptures to show that there is one God, the God of the Jews. In answer to my saying that one must not speak evil of gods, you added, to show that there is one maker, that those who did not make must perish. In answer to my saying that one must speak of gods, since the scriptures also speak of them, you showed that one must not utter their names, because the same scripture says not to utter the names of other gods. Since, then, the scriptures themselves speak of many gods and at other times of only one, and sometimes say not to speak evil of them and at other times to speak evil of them, what must we conclude from this except that the scriptures themselves mislead us?’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τί δεῖ λογίσασθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: what must we conclude
lexical_decisions.rationale: The question is about the inference required by the stated premises, retaining the necessity expressed by δεῖ rather than substituting mere ability.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλανῶσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: mislead
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term means leading astray or deceiving, not merely presenting a neutral diversity of views. Its accusation is retained as Simon's argument.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘They do not mislead; they expose, bringing into the open the evil intention against God that lurks like a serpent within each person. For they lie before us resembling many different impressions. Each person, having his own intention like wax, looks over them and finds everything in them. Whatever kind of god he wants to exist, he presses upon them his intention, which, as I said, resembles wax, and takes its impression. Since, then, anyone finds in them whatever he wishes to think about God, one person takes impressions of many gods from them. We, however, have taken the image of the one who truly exists, recognizing the true impression from our own form. Moreover, the soul within us is clothed in his image for immortality. If I abandon the begetter of this image, it too must abandon me by a just judgment, recognizing me as unjust from that very act of audacity. Coming from a just one, it will justly abandon me, and thus I shall perish in soul after punishment, when the help from it has departed. If there is another god, let him first clothe me in another appearance, another form, so that through the body's new form I may recognize the new god. But even if he changes the form, will he also change the soul's substance? If he changes that too, I am no longer myself, having become another in both form and substance. Let him therefore fashion others, if there is another. But there is not. If there were, he would have fashioned them. Since he has not fashioned them, being nonexistent, let him leave the one who truly exists alone. For there is no such one except in Simon's opinion alone. I accept no other God besides the one who created me.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τύποις
lexical_decisions.chosen: impressions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The scriptures' differing patterns are likened to forms that stamp wax. Impressions keeps the molding image that develops in the verbs of pressing and taking an imprint; types or models are lexical alternatives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτης τὸν γεννήτορα ἐὰν καταλίπω, δικαίᾳ κρίσει καὶ αὐτή με καταλιπεῖν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: If I abandon the begetter of this image, it too must abandon me by a just judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronouns are read as referring to the immediately preceding image in which the soul is clothed. The soul itself is a grammatically possible alternative, but the ensuing loss of assistance and destruction as to the soul favors the protecting image as what departs.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἀπὸ δικαίου δικαίως καταλείψει με
lexical_decisions.chosen: Coming from a just one, it will justly abandon me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase from a just one is read as the image's provenance from the righteous creator. A more literal alternative is and, as from a just one, it will justly abandon me; the main text does not make the unjust person just in order to remove the tension.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ψυχὴν μετὰ κόλασιν, τῆς ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἀπολειφθείσης βοηθείας, φθαρήσομαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I shall perish in soul after punishment, when the help from it has departed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative soul is taken as the respect in which destruction occurs, and it continues the image as the help's source. This conditional destruction is not softened into bodily death alone or harmonized with the later description of souls as immortal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἔστιν ἢ μόνῃ γνώμῃ. Σίμωνος
lexical_decisions.chosen: For there is no such one except in Simon's opinion alone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative concerns the proposed other god. The genitive Simon's completes opinion across the printed punctuation; no second speaker or missing sentence is invented.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Since I see you speaking so persistently on behalf of the God who fashioned you, learn from me how you are impious even toward him. The makers appear to be two, as scripture says, “And God said, Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness.” “Let us make” indicates two or more, but certainly not one.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural deliberative form and our are central to Simon's inference and retained. The second phrase does not repeat an expressed possessive, so the English does not add a second our.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘There is one who said to his own wisdom, “Let us make a human.” Wisdom, with which he himself always rejoiced as with his own spirit, is united with God like a soul, but extends from him like a hand, creating the whole. For this reason one human also came into being, and from him the female came forth. Though one in kind, it is a pair. For through extension and contraction the one is considered two. Thus I act rightly in rendering all honor to one God as to parents.’ Simon said, ‘What then? Even if the scriptures speak of other gods, will you not accept them?’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἥνωται μὲν ὡς ψυχὴ τῷ θεῷ, ἐκτείνεται δὲ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ὡς χείρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: is united with God like a soul, but extends from him like a hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both soul and hand comparisons are retained as the author's own account of wisdom. The rendering does not convert these comparisons into a later creedal definition or a separate independent creator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ μία οὖσα τῷ γένει δυάς ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Though one in kind, it is a pair
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine one and the noun pair can concern the human kind represented by male and female, with a possible continuing analogy to wisdom. The English leaves the collective referent broad instead of introducing a second named divine person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ γὰρ ἔκτασιν καὶ συστολὴν ἡ μονὰς δυὰς εἶναι νομίζεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: For through extension and contraction the one is considered two
lexical_decisions.rationale: The numerical unity and duality are translated into accessible English while preserving both spatial-process terms. A unit is considered a pair is a more technical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑνὶ θεῷ ὡς γονεῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to one God as to parents
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular one God and plural parents are both retained. The comparison is not silently normalized to one parent or expanded into two gods.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘Whether scriptures or prophets speak of gods, they speak to test their hearers. For it is written: “If a prophet arises among you, giving you signs and wonders, and that sign and wonder comes to pass, but he says to you, ‘Let us go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,’ you shall not listen to that prophet. Your hands shall be the first to stone him, for he tempted you to turn away from the Lord your God. If you say in your heart, ‘How did he perform that sign or wonder?’ you shall surely know that the tempter was testing you to see whether you fear the Lord your God.” It was said that the tempter was testing, but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon. For God, who knows everything, would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand, as can be shown from many passages. If you wish, we will discuss this, and I will show that God has foreknowledge. The claim that he is ignorant has been shown to be false and itself written as a test. Thus, Simon, we can neither be made to stumble by scriptures or anyone else, nor be deceived into accepting many gods, nor do we agree with any statement spoken against God.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γινώσκων γνώσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: you shall surely know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle plus finite verb repeats the knowing root for emphasis. The main rendering expresses that assurance without adding a new source of knowledge.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ πειράζων ἐπείραζεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the tempter was testing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated testing root is retained, with tempter distinguishing the agent from God in Peter's stated argument. The noun is not silently replaced by a personal name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως δὲ μετὰ τὴν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα μετοικεσίαν φαίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause asserts a difference in presentation after the Babylonian displacement. It does not specify a scribe, manuscript, or exact replacement wording, so none is supplied.

passages.text: ‘For we ourselves know from the scriptures that angels have been called gods: I mean the one who spoke at the bush and the one who wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God. Moreover, Moses became a god to Pharaoh, though in reality he was a human. So too the idols of the nations. But for us there is one God, one: the one who made created things and ordered everything, whose son the Messiah is. In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures. Moreover, supplied by the fathers with the true things of the scriptures, we know only one who made the heavens and the earth, the God of the Jews and of all who choose to worship him. The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us, so that we might know that anything said against God is false. But I will say something even beyond this: if things are not as I have said, may it be my lot, and that of those who love the truth, to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀγγέλους θεοὺς λεχθέντας
lexical_decisions.chosen: angels have been called gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following examples remain within Peter's statement about appellations. Their inclusion is retained without imposing or repairing the author's classification to fit a later theological system.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ καὶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱός, ᾧ πειθόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose son the Messiah is. In obedience to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Christos functions independently as a title, so Messiah follows the supplied policy. The relative him is grammatically compatible with the Messiah or God; the main text leaves the pronoun unexpanded rather than resolving that attachment silently.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: θεοφιλεῖ λογισμῷ ἀληθὲς ὂν δογματίσαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can mean God-loving or beloved by God. The argument's insistence on reverent thinking supports the active sense; reasoning dear to God is a material alternative. The truth qualification is retained without adding a new creed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ εὐφημίας τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἡμᾶς θεοῦ κινδυνεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The willingness to risk being wrong is explicitly tied to reverent speech about the creator. The translation does not turn it into a denial that any risk exists.

passages.text: When Simon heard this, he said, ‘Since you say that one must not believe even a prophet who gives signs and wonders but speaks of another god, knowing that he also deserves death, then your teacher too, who gave signs and wonders, was reasonably put to death.’ Peter answered, ‘Our Lord neither declared that gods exist besides the one who created everything nor proclaimed himself to be God. But he reasonably pronounced blessed the person who said that he was the son of the God who ordered everything.’ Simon answered, ‘Does it not seem to you, then, that one who comes from God is God?’ Peter said, ‘Tell us how this can be. We cannot tell you this, because we did not hear it from him.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε ἑαυτὸν θεὸν εἶναι ἀνηγόρευσεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: nor proclaimed himself to be God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The denial is retained as the author's Peter states it. It is not corrected or softened to conform to a denominational account of Christ's identity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν ἀπὸ θεοῦ θεὸν εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: one who comes from God is God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The origin phrase is rendered openly. God versus a god is a material English article alternative; the Greek argument concerns application of the divine designation rather than a newly specified rank in a pantheon.

passages.text: ‘Besides, it belongs to the Father not to have been begotten, but to the Son to have been begotten. What is begotten is not comparable with what is unbegotten or even self-begotten.’ Simon said, ‘Even if it is the same in respect of generation?’ Peter said, ‘One who is not in every respect the same as another cannot have all the same designations as that one.’ Simon said, ‘That is assertion, not demonstration.’ Peter said, ‘Why do you not understand that the one is self-begotten or even unbegotten, whereas the other, being begotten, cannot be called the same, not even if the begotten one is of the same substance as the begetter .... But learn this too: human bodies have immortal souls clothed in God's breath. Having come forth from God, they are of the same substance, but are not gods. If they are gods, then by that reasoning the souls of all humans—those who have died, those living, and those yet to be born—are gods. But if, persisting in your argument with me, you say that they too are gods, what great distinction remains even for the Messiah in being called God? For he has what everyone also has.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γεννητὸν δὲ ἀγεννήτῳ ἢ καὶ αὐτογεννήτῳ οὐ συγκρίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: What is begotten is not comparable with what is unbegotten or even self-begotten
lexical_decisions.rationale: The three generation terms and their distinctions are retained. Self-begotten is not silently collapsed into unbegotten, and the comparison is not rewritten to assert a later creedal formula.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εἰ καὶ τῇ γενέσει οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστιν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if it is the same in respect of generation?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The interrogative negative is read as seeking the admission that it is the same in respect of generation. More literally, Even if, in generation, is it not the same? Generation can mean coming-to-be or birth; the subsequent substance argument supplies context but does not erase the term.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς αὐτῆς οὐσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: of the same substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is retained both in the conditional argument about the begotten one and the subsequent account of souls. The passage's own distinction between shared substance and the title God is not harmonized with another theological position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ θεῷ λέγεσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: in being called God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied dative form occurs in the title-ascription expression. The English preserves the intended naming construction without supplying a further predicate or claiming to correct the printed Greek.

source_issues.issue: The edition prints four dots after the begetter clause. The English preserves exactly four dots, without supplying a missing verb or continuation. Its rendering of is in the preceding conditional clause provides ordinary English copular syntax and does not claim to restore the unavailable wording after the clause.

passages.text: ‘We call God the one whose distinctive property cannot belong to another. For just as he is called boundless because he is infinite in every direction, and it is altogether necessary, since another cannot likewise be infinite, that being called boundless not be a property of another—if anyone says this is possible, he lies, for two things infinite in every direction cannot coexist, since each is bounded by the other—so it is natural for the unbegotten to be one. Even if he has a shape, in this way too the incomparable is one. For this reason he is also called Most High, because, being above all, he has everything subject to himself.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ εἶναι ἴδιον τὸ καλεῖσθαι ἀπέραντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: that being called boundless not be a property of another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative is retained, and of another is inferred from the immediately preceding statement that another cannot likewise be infinite. If distinctive property is instead attached to God without that contextual complement, the clause appears to deny the distinctiveness it argues for. The main reading preserves the negation and supplies the contextually available referent, not a conjectural alteration of the Greek.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ δὲ ἐν σχήματί ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if he has a shape
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional concession is retained. The phrase does not deny shape in order to impose a different doctrine of divine incorporeality.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὕψιστος
lexical_decisions.chosen: Most High
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative title is translated and immediately explained by the source's claim of superiority over all.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Surely “God,” which everyone says, is not his unutterable name, that you insist so strongly even about the name, so that it may not be given to another?’ Peter said, ‘I know that this is not his unutterable name, but the one spoken by human convention. If you give this to another, you will attach the unspoken one to another too. In terms of intention, the spoken name is an advance toward the unspoken one. On this account the insult is reckoned also against what has not yet been spoken, just as honor directed toward what is known is referred to what is not yet known.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπόρρητον ὄνομα
lexical_decisions.chosen: unutterable name
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can denote a name not to be divulged or spoken. Secret name is another possible emphasis; the subsequent spoken/unspoken contrast supports unutterable without specifying the hidden name's letters.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ λεγόμενον ὄνομα τοῦ μὴ λεγομένου πρόοδός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the spoken name is an advance toward the unspoken one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The movement metaphor is retained. In terms of intention qualifies how assigning the public title implicates the unnamed divine identity; no separate name or magical utterance is supplied.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘I wished to know, Peter, whether you truly believe that the human form has been patterned after his form.’ Peter said, ‘Truly, Simon, I am fully convinced that this is so.’ Simon said, ‘How can death dissolve the body when it is patterned by the greatest seal?’ Peter said, ‘It is the form of a righteous God. When it begins to do wrong, the image within it flees, and so the body dissolves, in order that the form may disappear and an unrighteous body may not possess the form of a righteous God. The dissolution, however, concerns not the seal but the body that was sealed. The sealed thing is not dissolved without the one who sealed it. Thus it is not permitted even to die without judgment.’ Simon said, ‘What need was there, then, to give the form of such a one to the human raised from the earth?’ Peter said, ‘This happened because of the creating God's love for humanity. For in respect of substance everything is superior to human flesh—I mean the ether, the sun, the moon, the stars, air, water, fire, in a word, everything else too. These things, having come into being for human service and being superior in substance, gladly endure serving what is inferior in substance because of the form of the superior one. For just as those honoring a clay statue of a king have their honor referred to the one whose form the clay bears, so all creation gladly serves the human made from earth, looking toward that one's honor.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὰν οὖν ἀδικεῖν ἄρξηται, ἡ ἐν αὐτῷ ἰδέα φεύγει
lexical_decisions.chosen: When it begins to do wrong, the image within it flees
lexical_decisions.rationale: It refers to the body or embodied person under discussion. The distinction between the departing image and the dissolving sealed body is maintained, rather than replacing image with a named material organ.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄνευ δὲ τοῦ σφραγίσαντος τὸ σφραγισθὲν οὐ λύεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: The sealed thing is not dissolved without the one who sealed it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase does not explicitly name permission, presence, or action as the sense of without. The English leaves that relation broad; without the sealer's permission is a contextual explanatory alternative but adds an unexpressed noun.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ κατ’ οὐσίαν λόγῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: in respect of substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparison concerns what things consist of, not their moral worth. Its repetition distinguishes superior substance from the honor attached to the inferior human body's divine form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὴν ἐκείνου ἀφορῶσα τιμήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: looking toward that one's honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The king-statue comparison points to the superior original whose form the human bears. That one preserves the pronoun while the note identifies its contextual direction; it does not claim that earth itself is the king.

passages.text: ‘See, Simon, what kind of God you wish to persuade us to be ungrateful toward! The earth still carries you, perhaps wishing to see who would dare to think as you do. For you were the first to dare what no one had dared, the first to utter what we heard for the first time. We were the first and only ones to witness God's boundless patience in the face of such impiety from you—not that of some other god, but of the one who created the world, against whom you dared to be impious. No chasms opened in the earth, no fire was sent down from heaven or advanced to burn people, no rain was withheld, no multitude of wild beasts was sent from the thickets, and God's destructive wrath did not begin even against us because of one sinner, as in the case of spiritual adultery, which is worse than adultery according to the flesh. For is not the one who then punished sins the God who created heaven and earth? For even now, most grievously blasphemed, he would have inflicted the greatest punishment. But, on the contrary, he is patient and calls us to reorientation toward God. He has destructive arrows stored in his treasuries for the destruction of the impious, which he will release like living creatures when he takes his seat to repay his enemies with judgment. Therefore let us fear the righteous God whose form the human body bears as an honor.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἴσως δὲ ἰδεῖν βουλομένῃ τίς σοι τὰ ὅμοια φρονεῖν τολμήσοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: perhaps wishing to see who would dare to think as you do
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle is read as continuing the personified earth, despite its oblique inflection beside the nominative earth. Perhaps qualifies the conjecture; the English does not replace the earth with an unexpressed masculine observer.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ὁ τότε ἐπεξελθὼν τὰ ἁμαρτήματα οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς κτίστης θεός;
lexical_decisions.chosen: For is not the one who then punished sins the God who created heaven and earth?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed negative question is retained rather than turned into a categorical identification or categorical denial. Its relation to the following counterfactual punishment and contrasting patience is rhetorically difficult. A reading that challenges the attribution of the earlier punishments to the creator is materially possible; the main text preserves the question rather than deleting the negative or resolving the theology by emendation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς μετάνοιαν καλεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: calls us to reorientation toward God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied English policy uses reorientation for moral-spiritual redirection, with toward God where the context supports the destination. Here the creator's invitation contrasts with the preceding impiety against him; us is the contextually inferred addressee, not a claim that God himself must reorient.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: συντελοῦντα βέλη πρὸς συντέλειαν τῶν ἀσεβῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: destructive arrows ... for the destruction of the impious
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated completion or ending root describes final, destructive force. The English retains the destructive aim and the arrows image without supplying a specific weapon technology.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ζῷα ἔμψυχα
lexical_decisions.chosen: like living creatures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The life-bearing comparison is explicit; it does not say that the arrows are literally a named species of animal or angel.

passages.text: After Peter had said this, Simon answered, ‘Since I see you cleverly hinting that the things written against the creator in the books are not true, tomorrow I will show from your teacher's words that he says the creator is not the highest God.’ Having said this, Simon went out. Peter said to the crowds standing there, ‘Even if Simon can harm us in no other way concerning God, at least he prevents you from hearing the words that can purify the soul.’ At these words from Peter, much murmuring arose among the crowds, who said, ‘What necessity is there to let him come in here and speak his blasphemies against God?’ Peter heard and said, ‘May speech against God for the testing of human beings find its sufficient limit in Simon. For, as the Lord said, “There will be false apostles, false prophets, sects, and ambitions for rule.” These, as I conjecture, will take their beginning from Simon, who blasphemes God, and cooperate in saying the same things against God as Simon does.’ Having said this with tears, he beckoned the crowds with his hand. As they came forward, he laid his hands on them, prayed, and dismissed them, telling them to assemble earlier in the morning. Having said this, and groaning, he went inside and slept without even taking food.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν δημιουργὸν μὴ ἀνώτατον λέγοντα εἶναι θεόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: that he says the creator is not the highest God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The teacher is the contextually inferred speaker of the claim Simon intends to prove from his words. The creator remains the subject of the infinitive, not an explicitly named person newly introduced by the translation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Γένοιτο μέχρι Σίμωνος ἀρκετὸν γενέσθαι τὸν κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πρὸς πειρασμὸν ἀνθρώπων λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: May speech against God for the testing of human beings find its sufficient limit in Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wish concerns the sufficiency and limit of the testing discourse in Simon. May it suffice as far as Simon is a more literal alternative; the English does not change the wish into a prediction that no later blasphemy will occur.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἱρέσεις, φιλαρχίαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: sects, and ambitions for rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first noun can mean factions or schools and the second loves of ruling or power-seeking. Sects and ambitions for rule preserve both social division and desire for control, without assigning later denominational names.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition supplies this conjunction in editorial brackets. Its sense is translated as that, without claiming independent recovery of an unbroken witness.

The selected edition supplies the beginning of in the books within brackets, including part of the noun. The English translates the supplied complete expression; it does not invent additional lost wording or a dotted gap.

The selected edition brackets the completion of tomorrow and the following from. These supplied words are translated as printed; the translation is not a new reconstruction of their underlying witness.
